headline: Hot Inflation Report Pushes Rates Back Up
tileReason: September inflation came in hotter than expected, and rates jumped back toward their October high.
takeaway: Rates eased a little last week, then this morning's hotter-than-expected inflation report pushed them right back up. Over the next month, higher rates look a bit more likely than lower ones, but nothing is certain.

drivers.title: Inflation ran hot
drivers.text: Prices rose 3.7% over the past year, above the 3.6% forecast. Core inflation, which leaves out food and gas, rose to 2.6% against a 2.5% forecast. Gas jumped about 9% in a month, but the core number matters more because it shows price increases spreading. Bond investors sold, and the 10-year Treasury yield jumped about 9 basis points (0.09%).

drivers.title: Fed hike odds doubled
drivers.text: The Fed raised rates in September for the first time in three years. After today's report, traders see roughly even odds of another hike on October 28, up from about 22% yesterday, and a hike by year-end looks close to certain. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but expected hikes push longer-term rates up.

drivers.title: Oil prices eased early in the week
drivers.text: Oil fell Tuesday on expectations that more Russian diesel will reach global markets after a U.S.-brokered energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. Lower energy prices cool inflation fears, which helped rates fall to a two-week low before CPI.

drivers.title: The job market is cooling
drivers.text: Employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, far below forecasts, and unemployment rose to 4.2%. A softer job market usually helps rates, and that support is still in the background.

drivers.title: Strong demand for Treasury bonds
drivers.text: The 10-year yield hit a 24-year high of 5.365% on October 7, then eased after well-received government bond auctions showed investors are still buying at these levels.

outlook.basis: I lean slightly toward higher rates because core inflation was broad-based, the Fed has signaled more hikes, and markets now see an October hike as close to a coin flip. What keeps me from leaning further: the job market is clearly softening, and the gap between mortgage rates and the 10-year Treasury is wider than normal (about 2.20% vs. a typical 2.00%). If markets calm down, that gap can narrow and take some pressure off rates.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: Rates eased a bit last week, then inflation pushed them back up. If you're closing in the next 30 to 45 days, locking protects you from another jump. Ask your lender about a float-down option in case rates fall later.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates around 7.5% are stretching buyers' budgets. Pricing realistically, or offering a credit buyers can use to buy down their rate, can make your home stand out.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Rates dipped last week, then a hot inflation report this morning pushed them back up to around 7.5%. The next big test is the Fed's decision on October 28.
